title: Problem Documentation and Imports
content: The header documents Erdős Problem #1022. Property B asks: given a family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite sets, can the ground set be 2-colored so that no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is monochromatic? The problem imposes a *local density* (sparsity) condition—for every set $X$, at most $c(t)\cdot|X|$ members of $\mathcal{F}$ are subsets of $X$—and asks whether the threshold $c(t)$ can be taken to diverge with the minimum set size $t$. The file imports Mathlib's `Finset`, `Finset.Powerset`, `Fintype`, and `Tactic` modules.

title: Property B (2-Colorability)
content: `HasPropertyB F` is defined by the existence of a single set $S \subseteq \alpha$ (the 'true' color class) such that every member $f \in \mathcal{F}$ meets both $S$ and its complement: $f \cap S$ and $f \setminus S$ are both nonempty. This is exactly hypergraph 2-colorability stated via one subset of the ground set rather than a $\text{Bool}$-valued function—an equivalent but more economical encoding. `hasPropertyB_empty` and `hasPropertyB_subset` immediately follow: the empty family is trivially colorable, and Property B is inherited by subfamilies (the same $S$ works).

title: Minimum Size and the Sparsity Condition
content: Two core predicates parametrize the problem. `AllSizeAtLeast F t` requires every member to satisfy $|f| \ge t$—the parameter $t$ of the conjecture. `IsSparse F c` is the key structural condition: for *every* finite set $X$ (not just members of $\mathcal{F}$), the number of members contained in $X$ is at most $c\cdot|X|$. The universal quantifier over all $X$ makes sparsity a strong 'trace'-type bound on how densely $\mathcal{F}$ can sit inside any superset.

title: The Main Conjecture (Axiomatized)
content: `erdos_1022_conjecture` is the sole axiom and the only assumption in the file. It asserts the existence of a threshold $c:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ that tends to infinity—formalized as $\forall M,\exists t_0,\forall t\ge t_0,\ c(t)\ge M$—such that every $c(t)$-sparse family of sets of size $\ge t$ has Property B. The divergence clause is the mathematical heart of the problem: larger minimum size $t$ should permit progressively denser families to remain 2-colorable. The status is OPEN, so this is honestly carried as an axiom rather than a theorem.
mathContext: $\exists c:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N},\ (\forall M,\exists t_0,\forall t\ge t_0,\,c(t)\ge M)\wedge(\forall \mathcal{F},t,\ \text{AllSizeAtLeast}(\mathcal{F},t)\wedge\text{IsSparse}(\mathcal{F},c(t))\Rightarrow\text{HasPropertyB}(\mathcal{F}))$

title: Structural Properties of Sparsity
content: A block of monotonicity and degeneracy lemmas. `sparse_zero_forces_empty` shows a $0$-sparse family can only contain the empty set (taking $X = f$ gives $1 \le 0$ unless $f = \emptyset$), and `not_sparse_zero_of_nonempty_member` is its contrapositive. `isSparse_mono` (sparsity is preserved when $c$ increases) and `isSparse_subset` (subfamilies inherit sparsity) establish the natural order behavior. `allSizeAtLeast_mono` and `allSizeAtLeast_subset` give the analogous facts for the minimum-size predicate.

title: Base Case: A Single Large Set is 2-Colorable
content: `hasPropertyB_singleton` proves that a one-member family $\{f\}$ with $|f| \ge 2$ has Property B. The witness is $S = \{a\}$ for any $a \in f$: then $a \in f \cap S$ and a second element $b \in f \setminus \{a\}$ (which exists because $|f|\ge 2$) lies in $f \setminus S$. This is the simplest non-trivial instance of 2-colorability and serves as a building block for the matching and small-family results.

title: From Local Sparsity to a Global Size Bound
content: `filter_subset_card_le` bounds the subset count by $|\mathcal{F}|$, and `sparse_family_size_bound` converts the local sparsity condition into a global one: if every member is contained in some fixed ground set $U$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \le c\cdot|U|$. The proof observes that filtering $\mathcal{F}$ by '$\subseteq U$' returns all of $\mathcal{F}$, so the sparsity bound at $X = U$ applies directly. This is the bridge between the per-set sparsity definition and statements about the total number of members.

title: Element Degree in a Set Family
content: `degree F a` counts the members of $\mathcal{F}$ containing the element $a$, and `maxDegree F` is the supremum of degrees over the ground set. Degree is the 'local' counterpart of the global subset count: where sparsity bounds members inside a set $X$, degree bounds members through a point $a$. The lemmas `degree_subset` (monotone under subfamilies) and `degree_eq_zero_of_not_mem` record its basic behavior. Degree is the right notion for the corrected Lovász-type result in § 10 and the double-counting bridge in § 13.

title: Degree-Bounded Families and the Corrected Lovász Statement
content: `IsDegreeBounded F d` requires every element to appear in at most $d$ members. The file documents that the naïve 'lovász_theorem' axiom—claiming $1$-sparse $+$ all-sizes-$\ge 2$ implies Property B—was *removed* because it is false: the triangle $K_3 = \{\{0,1\},\{0,2\},\{1,2\}\}$ is $1$-sparse with all 2-edges yet is not 2-colorable. The genuine Lovász result uses the *degree* condition, which is strictly stronger than sparsity (see § 13). This correction is an important integrity feature of the formalization.

title: Matchings of Large Sets Have Property B
content: `matching_has_propertyB` proves that a degree-$\le 1$ family of sets of size $\ge 2$ (a 'matching' of hyperedges) has Property B. The proof is by induction on $\mathcal{F}$: degree $\le 1$ forces the new set $f_0$ to be *disjoint* from every previously colored member, so the inductive coloring $S'$ can be adjusted locally around $f_0$ (adding or removing one element of $f_0$) without disturbing the other sets. The case analysis on whether $f_0$ already meets both color classes is the technical core.

title: Sparsity and Size Under Union
content: `isSparse_union` shows that the union of a $c$-sparse and a $d$-sparse family is $(c+d)$-sparse, via `Finset.filter_union` and the union-cardinality bound. `allSizeAtLeast_union` shows the minimum-size predicate is preserved under union. These closure properties let one build complex families from simpler pieces while tracking the sparsity parameter additively.

title: Erdős 2^{t-1} First-Moment Bound
content: `erdos_first_moment_bound` is the headline proven result: any family of fewer than $2^{t-1}$ sets, each of size $\ge t \ge 2$, has Property B. The proof is a fully formalized first-moment / counting argument. The private lemmas `card_constOn_le` and `card_monochromatic_on_le` bound the number of colorings that are monochromatic on a given set $A$ by $2\cdot 2^{|\alpha|-|A|}$; a union bound over $\mathcal{F}$ then shows the 'bad' colorings number fewer than $2^{|\alpha|}$, so a proper 2-coloring must exist. This is Erdős's 1963 theorem, the global-size predecessor to the sparsity conjecture.

title: Degree-Bounded ⇒ Sparse (Double Counting)
content: `degree_bounded_implies_sparse` is the bridge that reconciles the corrected § 10 statement with the `IsSparse` framework: if every element has degree $\le d$ and every member is nonempty, then $\mathcal{F}$ is $d$-sparse. The proof is a clean double-counting argument. Fixing $X$ and letting $F_X$ be the members inside $X$: $|F_X|\le\sum_{f\in F_X}|f|=\sum_{x\in X}|\{f\in F_X:x\in f\}|\le\sum_{x\in X}\deg(x)\le d|X|$, where the middle equality swaps summation order via `Finset.sum_comm'`. Corollaries `matching_implies_sparse` and `degree_one_size_two_propertyB_and_sparse` confirm matchings of $\ge 2$-sets are simultaneously Property B and $1$-sparse, showing the degree condition is strictly stronger than sparsity.
